passage: Counselling note, Thursday. Chandrika, second-year commerce, came in after missing two tutorials. She sat on the edge of the chair and kept folding her bus pass. Her father has been in the district hospital for three weeks; she takes the night shift beside his bed, and the tuition classes she teaches in the evenings pay for her travel. She failed the accounts mid-semester paper and said, very quietly, "I am not lazy, I am just tired." She had already made a list: hospital, tuitions, college. I gave her the details for the student welfare fund and the peer study circle that meets on Saturdays. She wrote both on the back of her bus pass. Follow-up booked for next Thursday. — Vidya, college counsellor

Karthik's diary, 11 p.m.

Amma's chemo day again. I took Pooja to school, then went straight to the hospital, then the lab. I reached the circuits practical twenty minutes late and the examiner would not let me start. So that's a fail on paper.

Fees are due on the 15th and Appa's shop has been shut most of this month.

I sat on the hostel steps for a long time. Dilnaz came out with two cups of tea and didn't ask anything for ages. Then she said, "You know the department has a re-test rule for medical emergencies at home, right?" I didn't. She showed me the circular on her phone.

Tomorrow: 9 a.m., HoD's office, hospital letter in hand. Then the scholarship desk. Writing it here so I can't pretend I forgot.

I still feel like I'm juggling knives. But at least I've put two of them down on the table.

qa.a: Karthik reached the circuits practical twenty minutes late.

qa.a: Karthik felt overwhelmed and defeated, with a sick Amma, a failed practical and fees all at once, and later a little steadier once there was a plan.

passage: I sat behind Himani in the exam cell queue, so I heard most of it. She had a thin file with her audiologist's letter on top. When her turn came, she said, "I have moderate hearing loss in both ears. In the hall, I miss announcements, like time warnings and corrections to the paper. Could I sit in the front row, and could the invigilator write changes on the board?" The clerk said something about rules, and Himani didn't raise her voice. She just asked, "Who decides this, so I can send the letter to them?" Her ears went a bit red, and she kept tapping the file. I don't know if she was nervous or just impatient; with Himani, it's hard to tell. The clerk gave her an email address. Outside, she photographed the letter and sent it right there on the steps, then said to me, "Done. Now chai." That's all I saw. Monday. Vishal's first week at the design firm is a blur of sticky notes. Jahnavi, his lead, gives instructions in quick bursts during stand-up; by lunch he has lost half of them and is staying late to rebuild the list from memory. He tells no one about his ADHD.

"I work best when tasks are in writing, and when I'm not right next to the printer," he says. "I have ADHD. I'm not asking for less work, just a clearer way to receive it." Jahnavi nods slowly. "Would a shared task board after stand-up work?" she asks. "And the desk by the window is free."

When I was nineteen, my first-year classes were on the third floor, and my leg brace made the stairs take ten minutes each way. I was late every day. One professor marked me absent three times in a row. I was so angry and so ashamed that I nearly left the college.

Lab supervisor's note, week 6 of the summer internship.

Uday, our second-year intern, disagreed with me in today's team meeting. I had decided to drop all survey forms with a missing answer. He raised his hand and said, "Sir, may I push back a little? If we drop those forms, we lose most of the older villagers, because they skipped the online question. That could tilt the results." His voice shook slightly and he looked at his notes, not at me.

I asked him to show it. He had a quick count ready: two-thirds of the dropped forms came from people over sixty. I had not checked that.

We kept the forms and handled the missing answer another way. After the meeting, I told him the disagreement was useful and that he had framed it well. He said, "I was scared you'd think I was being rude." I've asked him to present the check next week to the whole group.

— Tushar

passage:
17 Feb

Got the history essay back: 11 out of 20, with "off-topic" in red across the second page. I was furious. Indu said, "Just leave it, profs never change marks." I nearly did.

But the question said "evaluate", and I had evaluated. So tonight I've drafted what to say at office hours, and I'm writing it here to practise:

"Professor Mathew, thank you for the comments. I'd like to understand the second-page mark. I read the question as asking me to compare two sources. Could you show me where I drifted?"

No "unfair". No "everyone else got more". Just the question and my reading of it.

Later —
I went. He listened, reread the page, and said I had a point about one section but not the other. Mark goes up to 13. Honestly, the marks mattered less than the fact that I said it out loud without crying or shouting.

Elizabeth, 1, fear of professors, 0.

qa.q: What mark did the essay get first, and what was it changed to?
qa.a: The essay first got 11 out of 20, and the mark went up to 13.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she first saw "off-topic" in red?
qa.a: Elizabeth was furious and felt misjudged, because she believed she had answered the "evaluate" question.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth do to keep her disagreement respectful?
qa.a: She practised her words, thanked the professor, asked him to show where she drifted, and avoided words like "unfair" or comparisons with others.

qa.q: How might the result have changed if Elizabeth had followed Indu's advice?
qa.a: She would have stayed silent and resentful, the mark would not have been reviewed, and she would not have learned she could disagree calmly.

grounding: A student disagrees with her professor's marking by preparing calm words and asking questions instead of staying silent or getting angry.

Okay, Disha, you asked how the running happened. So, I'm Wasim, and a year ago I was the person who bought running shoes and used them as a doorstop.

What changed wasn't willpower. I made it stupidly easy. I slept in my running T-shirt. The shoes stayed right beside the bed, laces already loose. The rule was only "put them on and step outside". If I came back after two minutes, that still counted.

And then the reward. There's a tea stall at the end of our lane. I only let myself have the cutting chai there after a run. Sounds silly, but by week three my feet were walking there before my brain woke up.

The harder part was killing the midnight scrolling. I moved my charger to the kitchen. First week, I kept getting up to check the phone and feeling like an idiot. By the second month I was asleep by eleven, and honestly, that did more for the running than anything else.

My sister Ritu used to drink three energy drinks a day in her first year of engineering. I share the flat with her, so I know the fridge.

In June, something changed. She stuck a paper chart on the fridge door with dates on it. Every day without a can got a green tick. She started keeping a steel bottle of lemon water where the cans had been, on the top shelf, right at eye level. The first week she was snappy in the afternoons and slept at odd hours. I asked if she was okay, and she said, "Headache. It passes." I couldn't tell if she was annoyed at me or at herself.

Then I noticed she'd set a phone alarm for 4 p.m., the time she used to buy a can, and she'd go for a walk to the park instead. By August the chart had a long green line. She hasn't said anything big about it. I'm Chaitanya, and I just stopped buying cans for the fridge too.

qa.a: She kept a steel bottle of lemon water on the top shelf, at eye level.

The acceptance email came at 2 a.m., and I read it standing in the hallway so I wouldn't wake Amma. A master's place in Bengaluru, with a stipend that would barely cover rent.

Two days earlier, the bank in Madurai had offered me a clerk's job. Permanent. Ten minutes from home.

Amma said, "Take the bank job, kanna. Your sister's wedding is next year." Sarita Chithi said the opposite: "She'll regret it forever if she doesn't go." Everyone had an opinion, and nobody knew what the course would lead to, including me.

So I made two columns on the back of a calendar. Not pros and cons, but "what I know" and "what I'm guessing". The guessing column was much longer.

In the end I asked the bank if I could defer for a year. They said no. I took Bengaluru anyway, and told Amma I would send part of the stipend home. I'm Kalyani, and I still don't know if I chose right. I only know I chose, instead of letting the loudest voice choose for me.

qa.a: The headings were "what I know" and "what I'm guessing".

qa.a: Kalyani felt uncertain and torn, still not knowing if it was right, but also some pride at having made the choice personally.

Tanvir met me today about the offer from the Dubai office. He brought two sheets of paper: one with the salary and visa details, the other with his parents' concerns, written in his own words. I found that unusual and thoughtful.

His father has asked him to stay in Lucknow for two years, because the family is planning his elder sister's move abroad after her marriage. His mother wants him to go. Tanvir said, "Whichever I pick, someone in the house feels let down."

He did not know yet whether the Dubai role had a path to promotion, or what the rent would be. I suggested he email the recruiter three specific questions before deciding, and that he ask his parents to talk it through together rather than one at a time. He looked relieved to have a next step.

I will see him again after he hears back. I did not tell him which to choose.

— Thomas Varghese

I coordinate the relief camp at the school in our ward, so I saw Arohi every day of the flood week. I'm Lalit, and I've seen a lot of college volunteers.

Most of them arrive wanting to hand things out and get a photo. Arohi arrived and asked the women from the colony how they wanted the rations shared. They said by family card, not by queue, because the elderly couldn't stand for long. She made a list and sat at a small table with the card numbers.

On the fourth day a news crew came. The others lined up in front. Arohi carried on sorting the damp rice sacks at the back. I asked her later why she didn't go. She shrugged and said, "It's not my flood."

I don't know what she was feeling underneath. She looked tired and her hands were cracked from the sacks. She came back the next weekend to help clean the classrooms, when there were no cameras at all.

qa.q: How did the women from the colony want the rations shared?
qa.a: They wanted them shared by family card, not by queue, because the elderly couldn't stand for long.

qa.a: Asking the affected people how they want help given, and then following their plan, makes the help fit their real needs.

qa.a: They would feel relieved and respected, since they no longer had to stand in long queues to get food.

Tuesday, after closing

Manoj bhaiya was off today. Not rude exactly, just short. "Fine." "Do it." No jokes about the milk frother, which he always jokes about. He also counted the cash drawer twice, which he never does.

My first instinct was to think I'd messed up the morning orders. I nearly asked, "Are you angry with me?" But he wasn't looking at me when he talked, he was looking at his phone every few minutes, so I guessed it was probably not about me.

So I didn't push. I just took the dishes without being asked and handled the loud customer at table four myself. Around six I put a cup of ginger tea by the till and said, "No pressure, but if you need to leave early, I can close."

He looked surprised, then said his father was having tests at the hospital. He left at seven. I closed alone. It took forever but I didn't mind.

— Jasleen

The milk cooperative in Shirol opens at six, and by half past, the queue of farmers stretches to the tamarind tree. Nitin has worked the testing counter for a year. Pallavi, who logs the readings beside him, usually hums while she writes.

Today she doesn't hum. She writes the numbers very neatly and keeps her face turned towards the ledger. When old Shinde kaka jokes about her handwriting, she smiles with only her mouth.

Nitin thinks of asking her right there, then stops; there are twenty farmers listening. Instead he takes over calling out the readings so she only has to write. At the tea break he sits a little apart, not too close, and says, "You seem quiet today. You don't have to tell me anything. I'm around if you want."

Pallavi is silent for a while. Then she says her marriage talks with a family in Sangli fell through yesterday, and the whole village already knows. Nitin just nods and passes her the biscuits.

qa.q: What does Pallavi usually do while she writes the readings?
qa.a: She usually hums while she writes.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's smile "with only her mouth" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she is hurt and embarrassed underneath, putting on a polite face in front of the farmers.

qa.q: Which of Nitin's choices helped Pallavi, and why?
qa.a: Waiting for a private moment and taking over the calling-out helped, because it reduced her load and avoided embarrassing her in front of twenty farmers.

qa.q: If you were Pallavi, what would you want from Nitin after she shares the news?
qa.a: Probably just what he did: to be listened to without questions or advice, and not to have the news become more gossip.

The promotion list went up on a Friday, and Vishal's name wasn't on it. He spent the weekend rehearsing complaints.

On Monday he did something else. He booked thirty minutes with Ankita, a senior analyst from another team who had once reviewed his dashboard and been blunt about it. At the café downstairs, he said, "I want the honest version. What would have made my manager say yes?"

Ankita stirred her coffee for a moment. "You do excellent work that nobody sees. You fix problems at midnight and never mention it in reviews. And in meetings you only speak when asked."

It stung. Vishal wrote it all down anyway.

"Would you look at my goals for the next six months?" he asked. "And if you think I'm ready by then, would you say so in the calibration meeting?"

Ankita laughed. "That's the first time a junior has asked me that directly. Send me the goals. We'll meet once a month." Vishal walked back upstairs lighter than he'd felt all weekend.

qa.a: The promotion list went up on a Friday.

qa.a: Vishal felt stung and a little hurt, but he wrote it down, showing he was determined to use it; later he felt lighter.

qa.a: He could share one problem he solved in each review, speak once in every meeting without being asked, and keep monthly meetings with Ankita.

qa.a: Ankita seems amused and impressed by his directness, and is willing to invest time as a mentor and perhaps a sponsor.

For my first two years at the firm, I thought good work would speak for itself. It didn't. I watched people with half my output get the interesting projects.

What changed was a lunch with Vikas, a partner I'd worked for exactly once. I asked him, rather clumsily, why I kept being passed over. He said, "Sonali, nobody in the room when projects are assigned knows what you want." That shocked me. I'd assumed everyone knew.

So I told him. I wanted to lead audit engagements for small manufacturers. He said he couldn't promise anything, but he'd mention my name when the next one came up.

Three months later, one did. He mentioned my name. I was nervous for most of that engagement and made two embarrassing mistakes, which he pointed out privately.

I'm leading my second one now. Looking back, the brave part wasn't the work. It was saying out loud, to someone with influence, what I actually wanted.

qa.q: What kind of work did Sonali say she wanted to lead?
qa.a: She wanted to lead audit engagements for small manufacturers.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel when Vikas said nobody knew what she wanted?
qa.a: Sonali felt shocked, because she had assumed everyone knew, and perhaps a little foolish for waiting.

qa.q: What could someone in Sonali's early position try, based on her story?
qa.a: Tell a senior person with influence exactly what role they want, ask them to mention their name, and accept private feedback on mistakes.

qa.a: Vikas probably sees himself as a sponsor who opened one door and gave honest feedback, while leaving the work itself to her.

The hardest conversation I had in my first year as a team lead was with Zeenat. She'd missed three deadlines in a row, each time with a cheerful message the night before.

I put it off for two weeks. I kept telling myself she'd sort it out. She didn't, and the rest of the team started covering for her and getting annoyed.

When I finally sat down with her, I said, "Zeenat, I need to talk about the last three deadlines. They were missed, and the team had to stay late. I'm not here to shout. I want to understand what's going on."

She went quiet, then admitted she'd been saying yes to work from two other managers because she didn't know how to refuse.

We made a rule: all new requests go through me. I checked in every Monday.

I'm Lalremsiami, and what I learned is that waiting two weeks was the unkind part. The conversation itself, done with respect, was the kind part.

qa.a: She had missed three deadlines in a row.

qa.a: Lalremsiami felt reluctant and uneasy, putting it off for two weeks while hoping the problem would sort itself out.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Delaying the talk let the team grow frustrated; stating the facts calmly, asking what was going on, and routing new requests through the lead fixed it.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt during the conversation?
qa.a: Zeenat probably felt ashamed and anxious at first, then relieved once she could explain that she didn't know how to refuse other managers.

Note for my records, Wednesday.

I watched Afreen's first month managing Ravi, the new trainee, and I want to note what she did well.

On day one she gave him a single task, the vendor tracker, with a written list of what "done" looks like. She didn't give him five things at once.

When he made errors in the tracker, she didn't fix them herself. She sat with him and asked, "Where do you think this went wrong?" and waited, even when he was slow. I could see her fingers tapping the desk, so I think the waiting cost her something.

In week three he was rude to a vendor on a call. She took him aside that afternoon, told him exactly which words were the problem and why, and asked him to call the vendor back. He did. She also told him privately that his tracker was now the best in the team.

I'll recommend her for the team lead programme.

— Deepika, operations manager

Kalyani put the draft contract on the table. "Before I sign, can we go through three things?"

Jyoti, the startup's founder, raised an eyebrow. "Sure."

"First, the scope. It says 'all design needs'. That could mean anything. Can we list it: the app screens, the logo, and two rounds of changes?"

"Fair. What else?"

"Payment. Right now it's all at the end. I'd like half at the start and half on delivery."

Jyoti frowned. "We're tight on cash this quarter."

"I understand. What about a third at the start, a third at the halfway review, and a third at the end?"

Jyoti tapped her pen. "Okay. That's doable."

"And last, if you want extra changes beyond two rounds, I charge per round. It's written at the bottom."

Jyoti laughed. "You came ready."

"I've been burnt before," Kalyani said. "I'd rather we both know where we stand, so we can still like each other at the end."

They shook hands.

qa.a: She asked to list the app screens, the logo, and two rounds of changes.
